articles.title: Fixing "unable to get local issuer certificate" in Claude Code, Cursor, Git & npm on a Work Mac
articles.excerpt: You set up Claude Code or open Cursor on your company MacBook, send your first prompt—or run npm install or git push—and immediately hit a wall: unable to get local issuer certificate UNABLE_TO_GET_IS…
articles.body: You set up Claude Code or open Cursor on your company MacBook, send your first prompt—or run npm install or git push —and immediately hit a wall: unable to get local issuer certificate UNABLE_TO_GET_ISSUER_CERT_LOCALLY self-signed certificate in certificate chain SSL: CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED Meanwhile, Safari and Chrome open api.anthropic.com , github.com , and registry.npmjs.org without a single warning. That discrepancy is almost always caused by corporate HTTPS break-and-inspect from a Secure Web Gateway (SWG) such as Zscaler, Netskope, Cloudflare Zero Trust, or Palo Alto GlobalProtect. Here is why your browser succeeds while your AI coding tools and CLIs break, and how to fix it cleanly on macOS without reaching for insecure shortcuts like NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0 .

articles.body: When the big AI labs introduced "computer use", the industry assumed desktop automation had finally arrived. Then developers actually tried it: It streams 2MB PNG screenshots across the internet every 3 seconds. It seizes your active foreground mouse cursor, moving it like a slow ghost. It eats 800MB–1.2GB of host RAM. A single elementary button click takes 35 to 60+ seconds. It costs $200/month or burns $0.15 per screenshot step. We asked a simple question: Why are we treating an operating system as a dumb raster image when Windows already has a programmatic accessibility state machine? articles.title: 11 Git tricks for reviewing what Claude Code and Codex changed on your Mac (2026)
articles.excerpt: Your coding agent says "Done!" and the working tree now has changes in files you never mentioned. Reading that diff is the part of AI coding nobody automates for you. These are the Git tricks and Mac…
articles.body: Your coding agent says "Done!" and the working tree now has changes in files you never mentioned. Reading that diff is the part of AI coding nobody automates for you. These are the Git tricks and Mac tools I'd use to review what Claude Code or Codex actually changed, keep the good parts, and throw out the rest. Before the agent touches anything 1. Commit a checkpoint first Run git add -A && git commit -m "checkpoint before agent" before you hand over a task. Now git diff HEAD shows exactly what the agent did, and undoing all of it is git reset --hard HEAD plus git clean -fd for any new files. Reading the diff 2. Start with git diff --stat Before reading a single line, see which files changed and how much.

articles.title: Air Velocity in Python: Twice the Speed Means Four Times the Fitting Loss
articles.excerpt: Air velocity in a duct is the easiest number in HVAC to calculate: V (fpm) = Q (CFM) / A (ft2) 200 CFM through an 8-inch round duct is about 573 fpm. Squeeze the same air into a 6-inch duct and it's a…
articles.body: Air velocity in a duct is the easiest number in HVAC to calculate: V (fpm) = Q (CFM) / A (ft2) 200 CFM through an 8-inch round duct is about 573 fpm. Squeeze the same air into a 6-inch duct and it's about 1,019 fpm. That part is linear in area and nobody gets it wrong. What people underestimate is what happens next. Every elbow, takeoff, boot and grille charges a toll, and that toll isn't proportional to velocity. It's proportional to velocity pressure , which goes with the square of velocity. Here's a short script that makes the effect visible. Velocity pressure in one line For standard air (0.075 lb/ft³), ASHRAE's duct design chapter gives: Pv = ( V / 4005 ) ** 2 # in. w.c., V in fpm The 4005 isn't magic.

articles.title: Retired AI models don't always fail loudly: luna-check now covers DeepSeek, xAI, Mistral, Cohere and Groq
articles.excerpt: Most people expect a retired model to return an error. Sometimes it does. Sometimes it quietly keeps working, just not the way you think. I just released luna-check v0.5.0, a small open-source CLI and…
articles.body: Most people expect a retired model to return an error. Sometimes it does. Sometimes it quietly keeps working, just not the way you think. I just released luna-check v0.5.0, a small open-source CLI and GitHub Action that scans your code for AI model names that are retired or about to be. It now covers 11 platforms and 429 model entries, including five new providers: Mistral AI, DeepSeek, xAI, Cohere and Groq. While adding them, I found that "retired" means very different things depending on the provider. Two kinds of retirement The request fails. DeepSeek's legacy names deepseek-chat and deepseek-reasoner stopped working on July 24, 2026 (15:59 UTC). Groq shut down llama-3.3-70b-versatile and llama-3.1-8b-instant on August 16, 2026. Mistral retires models on dated schedules too.

articles.title: Shot Lists, Last Frames and Idempotency Keys: Engineering a Short-Clip AI Video Pipeline
articles.excerpt: Disclosure: Written by the minimax3 team. We run an independent third-party MiniMax H3 (Hailuo 3) video generator and are not affiliated with, endorsed by, or operated by MiniMax or Hailuo. The first…
articles.body: Disclosure: Written by the minimax3 team. We run an independent third-party MiniMax H3 (Hailuo 3) video generator and are not affiliated with, endorsed by, or operated by MiniMax or Hailuo. The first time you build anything around a text-to-video model, it's tempting to treat it like a text API: send a prompt, get a result, done. That works for a demo. It falls apart the moment someone asks for "a 45-second product video," a retry fires twice, or a job fails at 2 a.m. Short-clip video models behave more like a render farm than a chat endpoint. Jobs are slow, they cost money, they have hard limits, and the output is a file you still have to inspect. This post is about the engineering around the prompt: planning shots as data, chaining clips through a last frame, and scripting jobs safely.

articles.body: " Star Trek: First Contact " celebrates its 30th anniversary today, and the engaging sci-fi classic still looks fantastic three decades later. With the sad passing of its star, Patrick Stewart , last month, and "Star Trek's" milestone 60th birthday taking place in 2026, this is a bittersweet salute that also holds an extra special significance. Directed by "The Next Generation's" Number One, Jonathan Frakes , in his feature film debut, " First Contact " consistently ranks as one of the finest "Star Trek" feature films among fans and critics, and those accolades are well deserved. Based on a compelling screenplay by Brannon Braga and Ronald D. Moore, "First Contact" remains as bright and beautiful as ever, brimming with bravado, heart, horror, and heroism.
articles.author: Jeff Spry

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov.22, 1989: NASA launches space shuttle Discovery on classified STS-33 mission for the US military
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 22, 1989, the space shuttle Discovery launched on the secret mission STS-33 for the U.S. military. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 22, 1989, the space shuttle Discovery launched on the secret mission STS-33 for the U.S. military. It lifted off from Kennedy Space Center and up into the dark of night. This was the third nighttime launch of the shuttle program and the 32nd shuttle mission overall. Discovery had five astronauts on board. Their mission was to deploy a classified payload for the U.S. Department of Defense. NASA and the military launched several secretive shuttle missions to deploy military satellites . The satellite that launched with STS-33 is believed to be a type of spy satellite called Magnum. But exactly what Magnum was doing in orbit remains classified. NASA's space shuttle Discovery launches on the classified STS-33 mission for the U.S. military on Nov. 22, 1989.
articles.author: Hanneke Weitering
